disease.name: Muscle Strain and Back Pain
disease.scientific_name: Musculoskeletal Strain / Lumbar Sprain / Non-Specific Low Back Pain / Mechanical Back Pain / Myofascial Pain Syndrome

overview.description: Muscle strain and back pain together represent the single most common cause of disability and work absence globally. A muscle strain (commonly called a 'pulled muscle') is an injury to a muscle or its associated tendon — ranging from microscopic overstretching of muscle fibres (Grade I) to a complete muscular rupture (Grade III) — caused by sudden excessive force, awkward movement, or chronic overuse. Back pain encompasses any pain arising from the spine, muscles, nerves, or other structures of the back. Low back pain (LBP) — pain in the lumbar region between the costal margin and gluteal folds — affects approximately 80% of people at some point in their lifetime and is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide. The vast majority (90-95%) of back pain is 'non-specific' — meaning no serious underlying structural or pathological cause is identified — and resolves with appropriate management within weeks. However, a critical clinical skill is identifying the small but important minority of patients with 'red flag' symptoms indicating serious underlying pathology (cauda equina syndrome, spinal malignancy, vertebral fracture, or spinal infection) requiring urgent investigation and specialist referral. Back pain is best understood through the biopsychosocial model — biological factors (disc disease, muscle injury, degeneration), psychological factors (depression, anxiety, fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophising), and social factors (work stress, poor ergonomics, compensation claims) all contribute to pain experience and chronicity.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the musculoskeletal system — lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine muscles, ligaments, intervertebral discs, facet joints, vertebral bodies; neurological structures — spinal nerve roots (radiculopathy), spinal cord (myelopathy), cauda equina; systematically in chronic pain — psychological and social wellbeing, cardiovascular fitness, immune function
overview.prevalence: Back pain affects 619 million people worldwide (GBD 2019 — the most prevalent musculoskeletal condition); 80% of adults experience significant back pain at least once in their lifetime; 10-15% develop chronic back pain lasting more than 12 weeks; leading cause of disability globally across all age groups; costs the global economy over $100 billion annually in lost productivity and healthcare
overview.age_group: All ages; peak incidence in adults aged 35-55 years; new onset in elderly >65 years warrants investigation for serious causes; adolescents — spondylolysis from sport; children — rare but schoolbag-related strain increasingly recognised
overview.is_curable_note: Acute non-specific muscle strain and back pain resolves completely in the majority (90%) of cases within 6-12 weeks with appropriate management. However, 5-10% of patients develop persistent chronic back pain which may be managed but not always fully cured.
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute back pain (<4 weeks) and subacute back pain (4-12 weeks) are generally not chronic; back pain persisting beyond 12 weeks is classified as chronic and requires a different management approach emphasising rehabilitation over passive treatment
overview.key_fact: The most important advance in back pain management in 30 years is the shift AWAY from bed rest and passive treatments TOWARD early active movement and exercise — staying active is the single most important message for acute back pain recovery

types.name: Acute Muscle Strain (Pulled Muscle)
types.description: A sudden injury to a muscle or tendon from excessive mechanical force — overstretching, a sharp twist, heavy lifting, or direct trauma — that overloads the muscle beyond its capacity. Micro-tears or macroscopic rupture of muscle fibres produces immediate pain, swelling, and restricted movement. The most commonly strained muscles in the back are the paraspinal muscles (erector spinae, multifidus), quadratus lumborum, and gluteal muscles.

grades.description: Microscopic overstretching of muscle fibres with no significant structural disruption. Fewer than 10% of fibres affected. Minimal swelling. Pain is mild — felt as a dull ache or tightness, worse with specific movements. Normal or near-normal range of motion. Muscle strength maintained.

Partial tear of muscle fibres — up to 90% of the muscle cross-section may be involved but continuity is preserved. Moderate swelling, tenderness, and bruising (ecchymosis appearing 24-48 hours after injury). Significant pain with movement and weakness. Palpable defect may be felt in the muscle. Restricted range of motion.
grades.recovery: 2-6 weeks with appropriate management; physiotherapy essential

grades.grade: Grade III — Severe Strain / Complete Rupture
grades.description: Complete tear of the muscle or musculotendinous junction — complete loss of structural continuity. Immediate severe pain at time of injury, often described as a 'pop' or 'snap'. Significant swelling and extensive bruising. Visible or palpable gap in the muscle belly. Complete loss of function in the affected muscle. Requires specialist assessment and possibly surgical repair.
grades.recovery: 6-12+ weeks; surgical consultation required for some complete ruptures

commonly_strained_back_muscles: Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis) — bilateral paraspinal muscles running length of spine; strained with lifting and twisting
Multifidus — deep stabiliser muscle of the lumbar spine; atrophies rapidly with back pain (first to lose function, last to recover)
Quadratus lumborum (QL) — lateral back muscle connecting 12th rib to iliac crest; strained with lateral bending, heavy lifting, or sudden twisting; a very common cause of acute low back pain
Gluteus medius and maximus — hip and pelvic muscles contributing to lumbopelvic stability; strain from sport or sudden movement
Piriformis — deep buttock muscle in proximity to sciatic nerve; can mimic sciatica (piriformis syndrome)
Thoracic paraspinal muscles — upper and mid-back strain from prolonged desk posture, carrying heavy bags, or sudden movement

types.name: Non-Specific Mechanical Low Back Pain
types.description: The most common type of back pain — accounting for 90-95% of all presentations. 'Non-specific' means no identifiable specific structural cause (disc herniation, fracture, tumour, infection) is found despite investigation. The pain is mechanical in nature — worsened by certain movements, postures, or loading, and improved by others. It arises from a complex interaction of muscle strain, ligamentous injury, facet joint irritation, disc disruption, and psychosocial factors. Prognosis is generally very good — 90% recover within 6 weeks.
types.characteristics: Onset often after a specific triggering movement (lifting, twisting) or insidious; predominantly lumbar location (between costal margin and gluteal folds); variable radiation to buttocks and upper thighs (referred pain — not true sciatica); pain worsened by movement, prolonged sitting or standing, forward flexion; often accompanied by muscle spasm; neurological examination normal; no specific diagnostic findings on imaging (or age-appropriate degenerative changes unrelated to symptoms)
types.natural_history: 70% improve within 2 weeks; 90% within 6 weeks; however, recurrence rate is high (50-80% have at least one further episode within 12 months); 5-10% develop persistent chronic back pain lasting more than 12 weeks
types.yellow_flags: Psychosocial risk factors predicting chronicity — fear-avoidance beliefs (fear that activity will worsen pain); catastrophising (magnifying the threat of pain); passive coping strategies (relying on rest and passive treatment); depression and anxiety; job dissatisfaction; poor social support; compensation claims or litigation; lack of control over working conditions; early identification and addressing yellow flags reduces chronicity

types.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation and Radiculopathy (Sciatica)
types.description: The nucleus pulposus — the soft jelly-like core of the intervertebral disc — herniates (protrudes, extrudes, or sequesters) through a tear in the outer fibrous ring (annulus fibrosus), compressing an adjacent spinal nerve root. In the lumbar spine, this most commonly affects the L4/5 or L5/S1 disc levels, compressing the L5 or S1 nerve roots and producing the clinical syndrome of sciatica — unilateral leg pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal distribution, often accompanied by neurological deficit.
types.anatomy: L3/4 disc herniation: affects L4 nerve root — pain radiating to anterior thigh and medial leg; weak knee extension (quadriceps); reduced knee jerk reflex. L4/5 disc herniation: affects L5 nerve root — pain radiating down posterior thigh, lateral leg, and dorsum of foot; weak foot dorsiflexion and big toe extension (foot drop risk); no reflex change (L5 has no reliable reflex). L5/S1 disc herniation: affects S1 nerve root — pain radiating down posterior thigh, calf, and lateral foot; weak plantar flexion (tiptoeing); reduced or absent ankle jerk reflex.
types.sciatica_characteristics: Typically unilateral; radiates below the knee into the leg and foot in a dermatomal pattern; severe burning, shooting, or electric-shock type pain; worse with sitting, bending forward, coughing, and Valsalva manoeuvre (increases intradiscal pressure); positive straight leg raise (SLR) test (Lasègue's sign) — pain reproduced by raising the straight leg to 30-60 degrees; may have associated paraesthesia (pins and needles), numbness, and weakness in myotomal distribution
types.natural_history: Most (80-90%) improve significantly within 3-6 months with conservative management; only 10-20% ultimately require surgery (microdiscectomy); prolonged sciatica with neurological deficit has worse prognosis
types.red_flag_within_type: CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME — central massive disc herniation compressing the cauda equina nerve roots bilaterally; presents with saddle anaesthesia (numbness of perineum, inner thighs, genitalia), bilateral leg weakness, and loss of bladder/bowel control (retention or incontinence) — SURGICAL EMERGENCY requiring MRI and emergency neurosurgical decompression within hours; incomplete recovery if delayed

types.name: Lumbar Spondylosis and Facet Joint Pain
types.description: Age-related degenerative changes of the lumbar spine — disc desiccation and height reduction (degenerative disc disease), osteophyte formation (bone spurs), thickening of ligamentum flavum, and osteoarthritic changes in the facet (zygapophyseal) joints. These changes are essentially normal ageing processes — present on MRI in 90% of adults by age 50 — and are NOT synonymous with pain; many people have severe MRI changes with no pain and vice versa. Facet joint pain is characteristically worse with extension and rotation, improved with flexion; aggravated by prolonged standing.
types.note: Over-reliance on MRI findings (labelling patients based on imaging rather than clinical picture) is a major driver of unnecessary fear, disability, and inappropriate treatment in back pain; the dictum 'treat the patient, not the scan' is fundamental

types.name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
types.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal (central stenosis) or the lateral foraminae (foraminal stenosis) from a combination of disc bulging, osteophytes, facet joint hypertrophy, and ligamentum flavum thickening — compressing the cauda equina nerve roots. Predominantly a condition of the elderly (peak onset >60 years). Presents with neurogenic claudication — leg pain, weakness, and 'heaviness' brought on by walking or standing (spinal extension narrows the canal further) and relieved by sitting or leaning forward (spinal flexion opens the canal). Often confused with vascular claudication (peripheral arterial disease).
types.distinguishing_from_vascular_claudicatio: Neurogenic (spinal): onset with walking AND standing; relieved by sitting or forward flexion; often resolves within minutes; may have neurological signs; peripheral pulses normal; ankle-brachial index normal. Vascular (PAD): onset only with walking; relieved by standing still; leg pain improves in <5 minutes standing; no neurological signs; reduced peripheral pulses; reduced ankle-brachial index (<0.9)
types.management: Conservative — physiotherapy (flexion-based exercises), NSAIDs, epidural steroid injections; surgical decompression (laminectomy/laminotomy) for severe or refractory cases with significant functional limitation

types.name: Cervical Strain and Neck Pain (Including Whiplash)
types.description: Strain of the cervical spine muscles, ligaments, and soft tissues — producing neck pain, stiffness, and restricted range of motion. Cervical strain may be acute (whiplash injury from road traffic accident — sudden acceleration-deceleration force; workplace injury; sport) or chronic (postural — prolonged screen use, poor desk setup, text neck). Cervical disc herniation (most commonly C5/6 or C6/7) produces cervical radiculopathy — arm pain, numbness, and weakness in the corresponding dermatomal/myotomal distribution (brachialgia).
types.whiplash_characteristics: Mechanism: sudden forced flexion-extension of the cervical spine (typically rear-end vehicle collision); symptoms may be delayed 12-48 hours; neck pain and stiffness, headache (occipital — cervicogenic), shoulder pain, dizziness, visual disturbance, difficulty concentrating (postconcussive features); Quebec Task Force Classification I-IV guides management; most (80%) resolve within 12 weeks; significant psychosocial overlay and litigation association
types.cervical_radiculopathy: C5/6 disc herniation affects C6 root — pain/numbness in lateral forearm, thumb, and index finger; weak biceps and wrist extension; reduced biceps reflex. C6/7 disc herniation affects C7 root — pain/numbness in middle finger; weak triceps and wrist flexion; reduced triceps reflex.
types.cervical_myelopathy: Compression of the cervical spinal cord itself (not just nerve roots) — a serious condition; presents with gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, upper and lower limb weakness, hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign; requires urgent MRI and neurosurgical consultation; may progress to permanent cord damage without treatment

types.name: Thoracic (Mid-Back) Strain and Pain
types.description: Strain or pain arising from the thoracic spine (T1-T12) and mid-back muscles. Less common than lumbar or cervical pain due to the rigid support of the ribcage. Common causes include: postural thoracic strain (prolonged desk work causing thoracic kyphosis and upper back muscle fatigue), costovertebral joint dysfunction (rib-vertebra joint pain — sharp unilateral pain worsening with breathing and specific movements), Scheuermann's disease (adolescent thoracic kyphosis from vertebral endplate changes), osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures in elderly, and thoracic disc herniation (rare). Thoracic pain should always prompt consideration of non-musculoskeletal causes — cardiac (aortic dissection — tearing chest-to-back pain), pleuritic (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism), and renal (pyelonephritis) disease.
types.important_differentials: Acute onset severe mid-back pain: exclude aortic dissection (tearing quality, hypertension, pulse differential, D-dimer/CT aorta). Mid-back pain with fever: exclude vertebral discitis/osteomyelitis or pyelonephritis. Thoracic pain worse at night unrelated to movement: consider malignancy

types.name: Sacroiliac Joint (SIJ) Dysfunction and Pelvic Girdle Pain
types.description: Pain arising from the sacroiliac joints — the large weight-bearing joints connecting the sacrum to the ilium of the pelvis. SIJ dysfunction produces low back, buttock, and posterior thigh pain. Particularly common in: pregnancy (pelvic girdle pain — PGP — affecting up to 20% of pregnant women from progesterone-mediated ligament laxity); post-partum; after falls directly onto the buttock; asymmetric leg loading sports. Often misdiagnosed as lumbar disc pathology or sciatica. Characteristic feature: pain provoked by specific SIJ tests (FABER, THIGH THRUST, posterior pelvic pain provocation test — PPPP).
types.note: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy is distinct from lumbar back pain — requires different management including pelvic physiotherapy, SI belt, and modified activity

types.name: Chronic Non-Specific Back Pain and Chronic Primary Back Pain
types.description: Back pain persisting beyond 12 weeks without a specific identifiable pathological cause — the most challenging and disabling form. The biopsychosocial model best explains chronic back pain: biological sensitisation (central and peripheral nervous system sensitisation — the pain system itself becomes dysregulated, amplifying pain signals beyond what tissue damage would justify), psychological factors (depression, anxiety, catastrophising, fear-avoidance behaviour, pain kinesiophobia), and social factors (poor work conditions, relationship stress, financial insecurity, social isolation). Structural findings on imaging in chronic back pain frequently do NOT correlate with symptom severity — chronic pain is a disease of the nervous system, not necessarily of the back structures.
types.management_philosophy: The modern evidence-based approach to chronic back pain centres on: active rehabilitation (exercise as medicine), psychological intervention (CBT, ACT — Acceptance and Commitment Therapy), pain education (explaining the neuroscience of pain — that pain is not always a marker of tissue damage), multidisciplinary pain management programmes, return to work support, and minimising passive and interventional treatments which reinforce disability and dependence

types.name: Serious Spinal Pathology — Red Flag Conditions
types.description: A critical minority of patients with back pain have serious underlying pathology requiring urgent investigation and specific treatment — not routine back pain management. These 'red flag' presentations must be identified at first assessment. Failure to recognise them can result in permanent disability or death.

red_flag_conditions.description: Compression of the cauda equina nerve roots (below L2) — typically from a large central disc herniation; also spinal epidural abscess, haematoma, or tumour
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: Saddle anaesthesia (numbness of perineum, inner thighs, genitalia); urinary retention or incontinence; faecal incontinence or constipation; bilateral leg weakness; sexual dysfunction
red_flag_conditions.urgency: SURGICAL EMERGENCY — MRI urgently within hours; emergency neurosurgical decompression; delay beyond 24-48 hours risks permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction

red_flag_conditions.description: Most commonly metastatic cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid, colorectal) seeding to the vertebral bodies; also primary spinal tumours (multiple myeloma, lymphoma, chordoma); vertebral body destruction can cause pathological fracture and spinal cord compression
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: Age >50 with new back pain; known history of any cancer; unexplained weight loss >10% in 6 months; pain worse at night (unrelated to posture — awakens from sleep); thoracic back pain; failure to improve with 4-6 weeks conservative treatment; multiple spinal levels
red_flag_conditions.investigation: MRI whole spine; plain X-ray (lytic/sclerotic lesions); FBC, ESR, CRP, PSA, serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP for myeloma), LDH, alkaline phosphatase, urine Bence Jones protein; CT-guided biopsy if lesion found

red_flag_conditions.description: Bacterial infection of the vertebral body and/or intervertebral disc — haematogenous spread from skin, IV lines, urinary tract, dental, or gut source; IV drug users at high risk; Staphylococcus aureus most common; Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pott's disease — spinal TB) is important in India and endemic areas
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: Fever with back pain; IV drug use; recent invasive procedure; immunocompromised; recent bacterial infection elsewhere; ESR and CRP markedly elevated; point tenderness over affected vertebra
red_flag_conditions.investigation: MRI spine (gold standard — shows disc and vertebral body signal changes); blood cultures (positive in 50-70%); ESR, CRP, WBC; CT-guided biopsy for culture and sensitivity; anti-TB work-up if Pott's suspected

red_flag_conditions.description: Fracture of one or more vertebral bodies — traumatic (road traffic accident, fall from height), insufficiency/stress fracture from osteoporosis (vertebral compression fracture — VCF — the most common osteoporotic fracture), or pathological fracture in malignancy
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: History of significant trauma; age >70 with acute back pain after minor trauma; known osteoporosis; long-term corticosteroid use; height loss and progressive kyphosis; acute onset severe mid-thoracic pain in elderly woman
red_flag_conditions.investigation: X-ray spine (loss of vertebral height, wedge deformity); MRI (detects acute vs chronic fracture, cord/nerve involvement, malignancy); DEXA scan (bone density); calcium, Vitamin D, PTH, bone markers

red_flag_conditions.description: Collection of pus or blood in the epidural space — compressing the spinal cord or cauda equina; rapidly progressive neurological deficit
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: Back pain with fever and rapidly progressive leg weakness or numbness; recent spinal procedure (epidural, discectomy); IV drug use; anticoagulation with back pain; septicaemia with back pain
red_flag_conditions.urgency: EMERGENCY MRI and neurosurgical consultation; evacuation within hours prevents permanent paralysis

red_flag_conditions.description: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) can cause severe back/abdominal pain from expansion or rupture — frequently misdiagnosed as musculoskeletal back pain. Aortic dissection causes severe tearing chest-to-back pain.
red_flag_conditions.red_flags: Severe sudden-onset back or abdominal pain in a patient over 50 (especially male smoker); pulsatile abdominal mass; hypotension; tearing quality of pain radiating to back

severity_levels.name: Mild — Grade I Strain / Minor Back Pain
severity_levels.description: Mild muscle overstretching or minor back pain with minimal functional limitation. No neurological signs. No red flags.
severity_levels.criteria: Localised back or muscle pain rated 1-4 on visual analogue scale (VAS 0-10); pain with specific movements but not at rest; able to perform most daily activities with mild modification; no radiation below the knee; no neurological symptoms; no red flags; normal gait
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild limitation of bending, lifting, or sitting tolerance; able to work (may need minor adjustments); can self-care
severity_levels.management: Self-management at home: remain active (avoid bed rest); short course of NSAIDs or paracetamol; heat or cold application; gentle stretching; reassurance; advice to stay active; no imaging needed; review if not improved in 2 weeks
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Pain worsening after 48-72 hours; radiation below the knee; neurological symptoms appearing; inability to perform self-care

severity_levels.name: Moderate — Significant Back Pain or Grade II Strain
severity_levels.description: Moderate pain significantly impacting daily activities, work, and sleep. Possible referred pain to buttock or posterior thigh (not below knee). No or very mild neurological signs.
severity_levels.criteria: Pain rated 5-7 on VAS; difficulty with activities of daily living (dressing, sitting, walking >15 minutes); unable to work or significant work restriction; referred pain to buttock or posterior thigh; muscle spasm on examination; possibly mildly reduced lumbar range of motion; no definite neurological deficit; no red flags
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to work in physically demanding roles; significant impact on recreational activities and social life; disrupted sleep
severity_levels.management: GP assessment; regular NSAIDs and/or paracetamol (scheduled, not PRN); short course of muscle relaxant if significant spasm; physiotherapy referral; reassurance and education; activity modification (not avoidance); review at 2-4 weeks; imaging NOT routinely required at this stage unless red flags develop
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Not improving after 4-6 weeks; neurological deficit emerging; pain radiating below knee; severe impact on all activities

severity_levels.name: Severe — Radiculopathy / Severe Functional Limitation / Grade III Strain
severity_levels.description: Severe back pain with sciatica (radiation below the knee in dermatomal distribution), neurological signs, or complete muscle rupture significantly disabling the patient. Requires specialist input.
severity_levels.criteria: Pain rated 7-10 on VAS; sciatica with leg pain radiating below knee; positive straight leg raise; neurological signs (reduced reflexes, myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory loss); complete functional incapacitation; unable to stand or walk; Grade III muscle rupture with palpable defect; uncontrolled pain despite analgesics
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to work; requires assistance with personal care; unable to drive; major impact on all aspects of life
severity_levels.management: Urgent GP or specialist review; MRI lumbar spine (confirm disc herniation and nerve compression level); neuropathic analgesics (gabapentin or pregabalin) for radicular pain; consider epidural steroid injection for severe radiculopathy; physiotherapy with specific nerve mobilisation techniques; consider surgical referral if no improvement after 6-12 weeks or worsening neurological deficit; Grade III strain — orthopaedic or sports medicine referral
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Cauda equina symptoms (bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia) — IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY

severity_levels.name: Critical — Red Flag / Cauda Equina Syndrome / Spinal Emergency
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening or spinal cord/cauda equina threatening condition presenting with back pain. Requires IMMEDIATE emergency investigation and treatment. Any delay risks permanent neurological deficit, paralysis, or death.
severity_levels.examples: Cauda equina syndrome (new urinary retention or incontinence + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg weakness); rapidly progressive motor deficit (acute cord compression); suspected spinal metastasis with impending cord compression; vertebral osteomyelitis with systemic sepsis; epidural abscess with neurological deterioration; aortic dissection presenting with back pain
severity_levels.management: Emergency department immediately; MRI spine within hours (not days); neurosurgical or spinal surgery consultation within hours; emergency decompression surgery for cauda equina or cord compression; IV antibiotics for epidural abscess or vertebral osteomyelitis; appropriate specialist management per causative pathology
severity_levels.outcome: Permanent neurological disability (bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction; paralysis) if delayed; excellent recovery if decompressed within hours of cauda equina onset

causative_mechanisms_overview.mechanical: The most common cause — biomechanical stress on spinal structures from poor posture, improper lifting, sudden awkward movement, sedentary lifestyle, and occupational overuse causing microtrauma to muscles, ligaments, and discs
causative_mechanisms_overview.degenerative: Age-related changes in intervertebral discs (desiccation, disc height loss, annular tears, herniation) and facet joints (osteoarthritis, osteophytosis) — the normal ageing process, but producing pain in susceptible individuals
causative_mechanisms_overview.inflammatory: Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis — HLA-B27-related; psoriatic arthritis; reactive arthritis) — presents with morning stiffness >45 minutes, improvement with activity, worse with rest, onset in young adults; treat entirely differently from mechanical back pain
causative_mechanisms_overview.neurological: Compression of nerve roots (radiculopathy from disc herniation, foraminal stenosis) or spinal cord (myelopathy from central stenosis, tumour, or acute disc herniation)
causative_mechanisms_overview.traumatic: Sudden acute injury — fall, road traffic accident, direct impact causing muscle tears, ligament sprains, fractures, or disc injuries
causative_mechanisms_overview.psychosocial: Psychological and social factors profoundly influence back pain — depression, anxiety, fear-avoidance behaviour, catastrophising, work dissatisfaction, poor coping strategies, and sleep deprivation all lower pain threshold and impair recovery; recognised in the biopsychosocial model

muscle_and_ligament: Muscle overuse and fatigue — repetitive tasks, sustained static postures
Sudden eccentric overload — lifting with back rather than legs
Poor neuromuscular control of trunk stabilisers (multifidus, transversus abdominis atrophy)
Direct trauma — blow to the back, fall
Poor flexibility — tight hip flexors (psoas), hamstrings, and thoracolumbar fascia increasing lumbar strain
intervertebral_disc: Repetitive compressive and shear loading — disc is avascular and heals poorly
Prolonged sitting (increased intradiscal pressure) — disc pressure is 40% higher sitting than standing
Heavy lifting with poor technique — especially combining lifting with twisting
Vibration exposure — lorry/tractor driving; jack hammers
Disc desiccation from ageing — reduced proteoglycan content reduces shock absorption
Smoking — impairs vascular supply to disc nutrition via endplate diffusion
facet_joints: Extension and rotation loading of spine — sport, gymnastics, overhead work
Spondylolisthesis — anterior slippage of one vertebra on the next causes facet stress
sacroiliac_joint: Pregnancy hormones (relaxin, progesterone) causing ligamentous laxity
Asymmetric loading sports (golfers, tennis players, throwers)
bone: Osteoporosis — post-menopausal women, prolonged steroid use, low calcium/Vitamin D
Stress fractures — spondylolysis (pars interarticularis fracture in young athletes)

risk_factors: Sedentary lifestyle and physical inactivity — weak core stabiliser muscles (multifidus, transversus abdominis) cannot adequately protect the spine under load
Prolonged desk work and sitting — sustained lumbar flexion for hours increases intradiscal pressure and fatigues paraspinal muscles; the most common occupational risk factor in modern economies
Poor ergonomics — poorly adjusted workstations, unsupportive seating, monitor position; prolonged driving (vibration + flexion)
Heavy manual labour — particularly with repetitive lifting, bending, and twisting; construction, nursing, farming
Obesity and excess body weight — increases compressive load on lumbar spine; BMI >30 doubles the risk of chronic low back pain; alters lumbopelvic alignment

Smoking — impairs blood supply to intervertebral discs (discs rely on diffusion through cartilaginous endplates); toxic effects on connective tissue; smokers have significantly higher rates of disc degeneration and chronic back pain
Age over 40 years — cumulative degenerative changes in discs and facet joints; age-related muscle mass reduction (sarcopenia)
Prior back pain episode — the strongest single risk factor for future episodes; recurrence rate is 50-80%

Psychosocial factors — depression and anxiety (3-fold increased risk of chronic back pain); high work stress and dissatisfaction; catastrophising (believing pain equals damage); fear-avoidance behaviour (avoiding activity for fear of worsening pain); poor social support
Poor posture and postural habits — thoracic kyphosis, lumbar hyperlordosis, forward head posture ('tech neck'), scoliosis
Improper lifting technique — bending from the back rather than squatting with the legs; twisting while lifting; sudden unexpected load
Poor physical fitness and core muscle weakness — inadequate trunk stability
Sleep deprivation — disrupts central pain processing, lowers pain threshold, delays tissue repair
Female sex — higher incidence of vertebral osteoporosis, pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy, and greater pain sensitivity
Tall stature — tall individuals with long lever arms have greater lumbar loading
Genetics — disc degeneration, spondylosis, and susceptibility to chronic pain have significant genetic components (twin studies show 30-60% heritability)
Inflammatory arthritis — ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27 positive), psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis
Previous spinal surgery — increased risk of adjacent level disease and failed back surgery syndrome

symptoms.overview: The clinical presentation of muscle strain and back pain varies enormously depending on the type, severity, and duration of the condition. The most important clinical task is identifying the pattern of symptoms that suggests serious pathology (red flags) versus benign mechanical back pain. Key questions: Is there radiation below the knee (radiculopathy)? Are there neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness, bladder/bowel changes)? Are there constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night pain)? Was there significant trauma?

primary_symptoms.name: Localised Back Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Aching, dull, stabbing, or burning pain localised to the lumbar (lower), thoracic (middle), or cervical (neck) region — the cardinal symptom. Mechanical back pain characteristically varies with posture and movement: certain positions or movements provoke the pain, others relieve it. Pain worsened by: forward bending (disc), extension and rotation (facet joints, spondylolysis), sitting (disc, sacroiliac), standing (spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis). Pain relieved by: lying flat (most mechanical), sitting (spinal stenosis). Pain UNAFFECTED by position and worse at night: concern for serious pathology (malignancy, infection).
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute (sudden — after movement, lifting, or twisting); Insidious (gradual — chronic overuse, postural, degenerative)

primary_symptoms.name: Muscle Stiffness and Spasm
primary_symptoms.description: Involuntary sustained contraction of paraspinal muscles — a protective splinting response to pain and injury. Muscle spasm causes visible and palpable tightening of the paraspinal muscles, restricted range of motion (especially lumbar flexion and rotation), and often a characteristic antalgic posture (list away from the painful side as the spine shifts to decompress the affected structure). Morning stiffness lasting <30 minutes is typical of mechanical back pain; morning stiffness lasting >45-60 minutes is a red flag for inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis).
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Prolonged muscle spasm itself perpetuates pain — a pain-spasm-pain cycle that can maintain symptoms beyond the original injury; muscle relaxants and gentle early movement break this cycle

primary_symptoms.name: Radiation of Pain (Referred vs Radicular)
primary_symptoms.description: Two distinct patterns of pain radiation must be distinguished: (1) Referred pain — dull, aching, poorly localised pain spreading from the lumbar spine to the buttock, posterior thigh, and sometimes to the knee. This is somatic referred pain from local spinal structures (disc, facet, SIJ) — not nerve root compression; does NOT radiate below the knee; no neurological deficit. (2) Radicular pain (sciatica) — sharp, burning, shooting, or electric-shock pain radiating below the knee into the leg and foot in a specific dermatomal pattern; caused by nerve root compression or irritation from disc herniation; may be accompanied by paraesthesia, numbness, and muscle weakness. The distinction matters — radicular pain with neurological deficit requires specific investigation (MRI) and management.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Radiation below the knee with neurological signs = radiculopathy — requires MRI; radiation only to buttock and thigh = referred pain — does not require imaging

primary_symptoms.name: Restricted Range of Motion (ROM)
primary_symptoms.description: Reduced movement in one or more planes of spinal motion — forward flexion (touching toes), extension (arching back), lateral flexion (side bending), and rotation — from pain inhibition, muscle guarding, joint stiffness, or pain-avoidance. The pattern of ROM restriction can suggest the involved structure: forward flexion limited and painful = disc or anterior ligament; extension limited and painful = facet joint, spondylolysis, or spinal stenosis; lateral flexion and rotation limited = muscle or facet. Schober's test formally measures lumbar flexion range; modified Schober's >5 cm increase in distance between two skin marks from rest to full flexion suggests adequate lumbar mobility.

primary_symptoms.name: Neurological Symptoms — Paraesthesia, Weakness, Numbness
primary_symptoms.description: Compression or irritation of spinal nerve roots or the spinal cord produces neurological symptoms in the distribution of the affected nerve. Paraesthesia (pins and needles, tingling) and numbness in a dermatomal distribution (L4: medial leg; L5: lateral leg and dorsum of foot; S1: lateral foot and little toe); Muscle weakness in a myotomal distribution (L4: tibialis anterior — foot dorsiflexion; L5: extensor hallucis longus — big toe extension; S1: gastrocnemius — plantarflexion). Footdrop (inability to dorsiflex foot — L4/L5 root or common peroneal nerve) requires urgent MRI and early management. Bilateral leg symptoms + bladder/bowel involvement = CAUDA EQUINA EMERGENCY.
primary_symptoms.severity: Moderate to Severe — any neurological deficit requires urgent assessment
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Progressive worsening neurological deficit is a relative emergency; static or slowly improving neurological deficit can be managed conservatively with close monitoring

primary_symptoms.name: Sleep Disturbance and Night Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Pain disrupting sleep — either difficulty falling asleep due to pain finding a comfortable position, or awakening during the night from pain. Night pain that is mechanical (worsened by turning in bed, relieved by getting up and moving about) is typical of muscle strain and inflammatory arthritis. Night pain that is CONSTANT, unrelated to posture, and not relieved by any position — particularly if waking from sleep — is a red flag for malignancy or infection and must be investigated urgently.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Persistent severe night pain unrelated to position = red flag; investigate for cancer or infection

secondary_symptoms: Generalised fatigue and malaise — from disrupted sleep, chronic pain, reduced physical activity, and depression
Depression and anxiety — extremely common in chronic back pain; lower mood increases pain sensitivity and impairs recovery; bidirectional relationship
Headache — cervicogenic headache (from upper cervical spine, trapezius, or suboccipital muscle strain); tension-type headache from neck pain
Swelling and bruising over injured muscle — particularly with Grade II-III strains; appears 12-48 hours after acute injury
Abdominal muscle weakness (impaired lumbopelvic stability) — following prolonged back pain; multifidus and transversus abdominis atrophy occurs within days of back pain onset
Antalgic posture — lateral trunk list (away from painful side), loss of lumbar lordosis (flat back — protective muscle splinting), or exaggerated lordosis
Difficulty with specific activities — prolonged sitting, standing, bending, carrying shopping, getting up from a chair, putting on shoes, sexual intercourse
Reduced exercise tolerance and aerobic deconditioning — from activity avoidance; a major contributor to chronic back pain disability
Joint stiffness in hips, knees, and ankles — from compensatory movement patterns and reduced activity
Bladder urgency or frequency — can be referred symptom from L1/L2 disc pathology; differentiate from cauda equina (which causes retention/incontinence)
red_flag_symptoms_requiring_immediate_ac: New bladder or bowel dysfunction — urinary retention (inability to urinate), urinary or faecal incontinence, or difficulty initiating urination — CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME until proven otherwise — GO TO EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IMMEDIATELY
Saddle anaesthesia — numbness or tingling of the perineum, genitalia, anus, or inner thighs (the 'saddle area') — CAUDA EQUINA EMERGENCY
Bilateral leg weakness or numbness — both legs simultaneously affected — CAUDA EQUINA OR CORD COMPRESSION EMERGENCY
Back pain with high fever (>38.5°C) and systemically unwell — possible vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess — URGENT ASSESSMENT
Sudden severe back pain in a patient over 50 with collapse or hypotension — possible ruptured aortic aneurysm — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY
Severe back pain after significant trauma (fall, RTA) in elderly or osteoporotic patient — possible vertebral fracture — EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Pain waking from sleep that is constant, position-independent, progressively worsening with associated unexplained weight loss — possible malignancy — URGENT GP SAME DAY
Progressive neurological deterioration — increasing leg weakness, spreading numbness — URGENT SPECIALIST ASSESSMENT within 24 hours
Back pain in a known cancer patient — possible metastatic spinal disease — URGENT SAME-DAY ONCOLOGY OR EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT
Back pain with fever in an IV drug user or immunocompromised patient — possible epidural abscess or discitis — EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
yellow_flag_symptoms_predicting_chronic_: Belief that all back pain is harmful and that activity will cause further damage
Catastrophising language — 'my back is broken', 'I'll never get better', 'this is the worst thing that could happen'
Fear of movement (kinesiophobia) — avoiding all activity or movement because of pain
Passive coping — waiting for treatment to 'fix' the pain rather than active self-management
Social withdrawal and isolation from pain
Expectation that a scan or treatment will reveal and fix an exact structural cause
Work-related stress, job dissatisfaction, or fear of returning to work
Sleep disturbance predominantly from anxiety about pain rather than pain itself

medical_history: Location of pain — lumbar, thoracic, cervical; precise localisation including any radiation; unilateral vs bilateral
Onset — sudden (acute trauma/strain) vs insidious (chronic/degenerative); specific triggering event (lifting, twisting, bending, sitting for hours, RTA, fall)
Character of pain — dull/aching (muscle, facet), sharp/burning/shooting (radicular), constant (serious pathology), colicky (visceral referred)
Radiation — below the knee with neurological symptoms = radiculopathy; buttock and thigh only = referred; bilateral radiation with bladder/bowel changes = CAUDA EQUINA
Neurological symptoms — paraesthesia, numbness, weakness in legs or arms; bladder and bowel function (CRITICAL — any change requires urgent assessment)
Aggravating and relieving factors — forward flexion (disc), extension (facet/stenosis), sitting (disc), lying flat (most mechanical); POSITIONAL RELIEF excludes serious pathology
Night pain — does position change relieve it? (mechanical) or is it constant and position-independent? (red flag for cancer/infection)

Red flag screening — constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats), history of cancer, age >50 with new back pain, trauma, immunosuppression, IV drug use, prolonged steroid use (osteoporosis)
Yellow flag screening — beliefs about pain (is it harmful?), fear of movement, work situation, mood (PHQ-2 depression screen), sleep quality, previous episodes and how they resolved
Duration — acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), chronic (>12 weeks); chronicity changes management approach
Previous episodes — frequency, duration, what helped, what did not help; prior investigations and their results
Previous treatments — physiotherapy (what type, how many sessions, compliance, outcome); medications tried (which ones, response); injections; surgery
Occupational history — type of work (manual, desk, driving); hours of sitting; heavy lifting; work absence; compensation claim
Social history — impact on daily life, exercise, hobbies, relationships, sleep; social support
Medical history — osteoporosis, cancer, inflammatory arthritis, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety; steroid use
Family history — inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis — HLA-B27-related); osteoporosis

Review of systems — inflammatory back pain features: morning stiffness >45 minutes, improvement with activity, worse with rest, associated uveitis, heel pain (enthesitis), skin rash (psoriasis), diarrhoea (IBD-related arthropathy)
physical_examination: Inspection — gait (antalgic, foot drop); posture (lumbar lordosis — increased/reduced/absent, thoracic kyphosis, lateral list, scoliosis); muscle wasting; swelling or bruising over injury site

Range of motion — assess lumbar flexion (modified Schober's test: marks at S2 and 10 cm above; <5 cm increase = reduced; inability to touch toes); extension; lateral flexion; rotation; note pain provocation with each movement

Palpation — midline spinous process tenderness (fracture, discitis — point tenderness); paraspinal muscle tenderness and spasm (bilateral = muscle, unilateral = facet/disc); SIJ tenderness; sciatic notch tenderness (piriformis syndrome); coccygeal tenderness

Neurological examination — ESSENTIAL in all back pain; lower limb: tone, power (hip flexors L1/2; knee extension L3/4; foot dorsiflexion L4/5; big toe extension L5; plantarflexion S1/2); sensation (dermatomes L1-S3 mapped); reflexes (knee jerk L3/4; ankle jerk S1/2 — reduced or absent = nerve root compression); Babinski sign (extensor plantar response = upper motor neuron/cord involvement)

Straight Leg Raise (SLR) / Lasègue's Test — with patient supine, raise the straight leg passively; positive if pain radiates below the knee (NOT just back pain) at 30-60 degrees; highly sensitive (90%) for L4/5 or L5/S1 disc herniation; must be distinguished from hamstring tightness
Crossed SLR (contralateral SLR) — pain in symptomatic leg when CONTRALATERAL leg is raised; highly specific (88%) for disc herniation
Femoral Nerve Stretch Test — patient prone, flex knee; positive if pain radiates down front of thigh = L3/4 nerve root involvement; tests upper lumbar disc herniation

FABER / Patrick Test (Flexion ABduction External Rotation) — hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated (figure-of-4 position); pain in groin = hip pathology; pain in sacroiliac region = SIJ dysfunction
SIJ Provocation Tests — THIGH THRUST, Posterior Pelvic Pain Provocation (PPPP), Gaenslen's test; positive = SIJ as pain source

Waddell's Non-Organic Signs — 5 clinical signs (tenderness to light touch, simulation tests — axial loading on head, rotation of pelvis en bloc; distraction test — SLR performed distracted vs formally; regional sensory/motor non-anatomical changes; overreaction); 3 or more positive = significant non-organic/psychological component to pain (neither faking nor malingering — indicates significant distress and need for psychological evaluation)

Slump Test — sitting, slump forward, extend knee, dorsiflex foot; positive if sciatic pain reproduced and relieved by cervical extension (confirms neural tension component); sensitive for disc herniation with radiculopathy
Abdominal examination — pulsatile abdominal mass (aortic aneurysm in over-50s with sudden back pain); renal angle tenderness (pyelonephritis mimicking back pain)
Rectal tone assessment — in suspected cauda equina syndrome (reduced anal tone = sacral nerve root dysfunction); perianal sensation assessment

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Plain X-Ray of the Spine (Lumbar, Thoracic, or Cervical)
diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging for back pain when investigation is indicated — primarily for detecting bony pathology. Shows vertebral body alignment, fractures, disc space height (indirect indication of disc disease), osteophytes, vertebral endplate changes, spondylolisthesis (forward slippage assessed on lateral view), sacroiliac joint erosions (ankylosing spondylitis — 'bamboo spine'), and gross destructive lesions from malignancy. However, X-rays do NOT show the intervertebral discs, spinal cord, nerve roots, or soft tissues — MRI is required for these.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect vertebral fracture (acute trauma, osteoporosis, pathological); spondylolisthesis; spondylolysis (pars defect — best seen on oblique views); gross malignancy; spondylitis/osteomyelitis (late changes); assess alignment and vertebral height
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Loss of vertebral body height >20% = vertebral compression fracture; intervertebral disc space narrowing + endplate erosion + adjacent vertebrae = discitis; 'Scottie dog' sign on oblique view — pars defect ('broken collar') = spondylolysis
diagnostic_tests.indication: Significant trauma (possible fracture); suspected malignancy or infection; spondylolysis in young athlete; spondylolisthesis assessment; ankylosing spondylitis workup (sacroiliac joints on AP pelvis view)
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Does NOT show disc herniation, nerve root compression, spinal cord, soft tissue inflammation, or early malignancy — MRI needed for these; most MRI-confirmed disc herniations cause normal X-rays; age-related degeneration changes on X-ray are extremely prevalent and often clinically insignificant
diagnostic_tests.note: Routine X-ray is NOT recommended for uncomplicated acute back pain without red flags — does not change management, irradiates the patient, and may generate unhelpful anxiety from incidental age-related findings

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI of the Spine (Lumbar, Thoracic, or Cervical)
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard investigation for structural causes of back pain — provides unrivalled soft tissue detail: disc morphology (herniation type and degree — bulge, protrusion, extrusion, sequestration), nerve root compression (direct visualisation of nerve root contact and displacement), spinal cord signal changes (myelopathy), spinal canal diameter (stenosis), vertebral body signal (bone marrow oedema from fracture — bright on STIR or T2; malignant infiltration; discitis/osteomyelitis — T2 signal change and enhancement), epidural collections (abscess, haematoma), and soft tissue masses. Does NOT use ionising radiation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm disc herniation and nerve root level affected (guiding injection or surgery); diagnose cauda equina syndrome urgently; detect malignant spinal disease; diagnose vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess; pre-surgical planning; persistent neurological deficit after conservative management
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Disc herniation grading: bulge (disc extends beyond endplates symmetrically); protrusion (focal herniation with base wider than apex); extrusion (base narrower than neck — fragment prolapsed into canal); sequestration (free disc fragment detached from parent disc). T2 hypointense disc = desiccated degenerate disc; T2 hyperintense disc or adjacent bone marrow = acute injury, infection, or tumour
diagnostic_tests.indication: Any red flag symptoms (immediate emergency); cauda equina symptoms (within hours); significant neurological deficit; sciatica not improving after 6-8 weeks; prior to epidural steroid injection or surgery; suspected malignancy, infection, or fracture
diagnostic_tests.critical_caveat: MRI FINDINGS COMMONLY FOUND IN ASYMPTOMATIC PEOPLE and do NOT imply clinically significant pathology: disc bulges (present in 64% of asymptomatic 40-year-olds), disc herniations (present in 32% of asymptomatic adults), disc degeneration (present in 91% of asymptomatic 60-year-olds). TREAT THE PATIENT, NOT THE SCAN. An abnormal MRI does NOT confirm that the finding causes the patient's pain. Over-investigation with MRI in uncomplicated back pain without red flags is associated with worse outcomes (increased fear, more surgery, more disability) — this is a well-documented harmful practice.

diagnostic_tests.description: Provides superior bony detail compared to MRI — ideal for complex fracture characterisation, surgical planning, and assessment of bony canal dimensions in spinal stenosis. CT myelogram (CT with intrathecal contrast) is used when MRI is contraindicated (pacemaker, metal implants).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Vertebral fracture characterisation (type, displacement, stability); bony detail in spinal stenosis; surgical planning for complex deformity; spondylolysis (pars defect — CT is more sensitive than plain X-ray); pedicle screw trajectory planning
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TLICS (Thoracolumbar Injury Classification System) guides fracture management; spondylolysis — 'bone defect' in the pars interarticularis on axial CT
diagnostic_tests.note: CT has significant radiation dose — consider MRI preferentially in younger patients and when soft tissue detail is required

diagnostic_tests.description: EMG measures the electrical activity of muscles at rest and during contraction — denervation changes (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) indicate nerve root or peripheral nerve injury. NCS measures the speed and amplitude of conduction along peripheral nerves — reduces in neuropathy. Together they localise and characterise nerve root pathology, help distinguish radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy, and provide prognostic information for recovery.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm and localise radiculopathy; distinguish disc herniation radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy or plexopathy; assess severity and prognosis of nerve root injury; assist pre-surgical planning; determine if neurological deficit is acute (new denervation) or chronic (reinnervation)
diagnostic_tests.indication: Neurological deficit of uncertain cause; atypical radiculopathy pattern; differentiating lumbar radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy (diabetic neuropathy, peroneal nerve palsy — all causing foot drop)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves: acute denervation (2-3 weeks after nerve injury); polyphasic motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment: chronic radiculopathy; reduced SNAP (sensory nerve action potential): peripheral nerve or dorsal root ganglion pathology

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Tests — FBC, ESR, CRP, Biochemistry
diagnostic_tests.description: Routine blood tests are NOT required for non-specific mechanical back pain without red flags. They are essential when red flag pathology is suspected.

tests_and_indications.purpose: Anaemia (malignancy, blood loss from fracture); leucocytosis (infection — vertebral osteomyelitis, epidural abscess); thrombocytopenia (bone marrow involvement from malignancy)

Very elevated ESR and CRP (>50-100 mm/hr) = infection (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis) or malignancy; normal ESR effectively excludes infection and most malignancy; also elevated in inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis)
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer to metastasise to the lumbar spine in men; check in all men >50 with new-onset back pain without a clear mechanical cause

tests_and_indications.test: Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) and Urine Bence Jones Protein
tests_and_indications.purpose: Multiple myeloma — the most common primary malignant bone tumour; typically affects vertebral bodies; presents with back pain and may show paraprotein band on SPEP; Bence Jones protein in urine; elevated serum calcium and immunoglobulin
Elevated in bone metastases (ALP); lymphoma and widespread malignancy (LDH)
Hypercalcaemia — malignancy (bone metastases releasing calcium), primary hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma; bone pain and systemic symptoms

Inflammatory spondyloarthropathy — ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis; positive in 90-95% of ankylosing spondylitis but also in 8-10% of general population; interpret with clinical context
Vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess with systemic sepsis — take before antibiotics

Vitamin D deficiency (common in India) causes musculoskeletal pain that mimics mechanical back pain; osteomalacia (adult Vitamin D deficiency) presents with diffuse bone and muscle pain and proximal weakness; check in all patients with persistent back pain and fatigue
Hypothyroidism causes generalised musculoskeletal pain, myopathy, and fatigue mimicking back pain — check TSH if fatigue and diffuse muscle pain are prominent

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine (L1-L4), femoral neck, and total hip. T-score compares to peak bone mass in young adults: T-score above -1.0 = normal; T-score -1.0 to -2.5 = osteopenia; T-score below -2.5 = osteoporosis. FRAX score uses DEXA + clinical risk factors to calculate 10-year absolute risk of major osteoporotic fracture — guides treatment decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose osteoporosis in patients with vertebral fracture or high risk; guide bisphosphonate/anti-osteoporotic therapy; assess Vitamin D and calcium therapy response; monitor treatment
diagnostic_tests.indication: Vertebral compression fracture on X-ray; women over 65 years; men over 70 years; postmenopausal women with additional risk factors; long-term corticosteroid use (>3 months); low trauma fracture at any age; malabsorption syndromes; hypogonadism

diagnostic_tests.description: Whole-body scan detecting areas of increased bone metabolic activity (hot spots) from fracture, malignancy, infection, or Paget's disease. Highly sensitive but low specificity — identifies any area of increased bone turnover. Useful for screening for occult fracture (spondylolysis, stress fracture), multifocal bone metastases, and vertebral osteomyelitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for bone metastases (multiple hot spots); detect acute fracture when X-ray normal; identify spondylolysis; evaluate Paget's disease; vertebral osteomyelitis (early — before X-ray changes); distinguish benign from malignant compression fractures
diagnostic_tests.note: SPECT (Single Photon Emission CT) bone scan gives more anatomical localisation than planar scan; SPECT/CT combines functional and anatomical information

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Diagnostic Nerve Root Block and Medial Branch Block
diagnostic_tests.description: Image-guided (fluoroscopy or CT) injection of local anaesthetic around a specific nerve root or facet joint medial branch nerve. Used to confirm the clinical level of pain — if injection at a specific level provides significant pain relief (>50-70% reduction), that level is confirmed as the pain generator. Guides treatment decisions — particularly for surgical planning and targeted therapeutic injections.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm pain generator level before surgery or radiofrequency ablation; distinguish L4, L5, or S1 radiculopathy when MRI shows multi-level changes; facet joint medial branch block to confirm facet pain before radiofrequency denervation
diagnostic_tests.note: Purely diagnostic — local anaesthetic effect temporary (hours); provides no long-term treatment benefit; must be combined with therapeutic plan

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Ultrasound of Paraspinal Muscles and Tendons
diagnostic_tests.description: Real-time imaging of superficial muscles and tendons — useful for detecting muscle tears (Grade II-III strains), haematoma formation, tendon pathology, and guiding therapeutic injections (trigger point, SIJ) in musculoskeletal back pain. Real-time visualisation of muscle contraction provides biofeedback during rehabilitation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm muscle tear or haematoma in acute strain; guide injection therapy (trigger point, piriformis, SIJ); assess multifidus muscle cross-sectional area (reduced multifidus = prognostic marker for recurrent LBP); guide nerve blocks
diagnostic_tests.note: Cannot image deep spinal structures (disc, cord) — limited to superficial soft tissue assessment

medicines.note: The most important principle in back pain management is that analgesics provide temporary pain relief to FACILITATE rehabilitation — they are not the primary treatment. The best evidence supports early return to normal activities and structured exercise. Medications should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary period. Paracetamol alone has limited evidence for acute LBP — NSAIDs are more effective. Opioids have significant risks and modest benefits and should be avoided for routine back pain. Never use opioids as first-line therapy for non-specific mechanical back pain.
treatment_principles: 1. STAY ACTIVE — the most important instruction for acute back pain; avoiding activity delays recovery and predicts chronicity; gentle walking and normal activities as tolerated should begin immediately

2. NSAIDs are the most effective first-line analgesics for back pain — more effective than paracetamol alone; use at full therapeutic doses for short courses; always prescribe with gastroprotection (PPI) if using for more than 5 days

3. Muscle relaxants are useful short-term (maximum 5-7 days) for painful muscle spasm — they are sedating and carry dependency risk; diazepam specifically should be used with caution and for maximum 5 days
4. Topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel, ibuprofen gel) are effective for localised back pain with fewer systemic side effects than oral NSAIDs — first-line for mild-moderate localised pain
5. Neuropathic agents (gabapentin, pregabalin) are indicated ONLY for radicular pain (sciatica) — they are NOT effective for non-specific mechanical back pain and should not be prescribed for it

6. Opioids should be AVOIDED for routine non-specific back pain — evidence for benefit beyond 4-8 weeks is very poor; risks of addiction, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and long-term disability are significant
7. Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine) have evidence for chronic back pain — both for pain relief and for treating the commonly co-existing depression and sleep disturbance

8. Vitamin D deficiency should be corrected in all patients with musculoskeletal back pain — Vitamin D deficiency (extremely common in India and South Asia) causes diffuse musculoskeletal pain, proximal muscle weakness, and fatigue
9. Medications should be reviewed at every appointment — dose reduction and discontinuation plan should be discussed from the start

categories.purpose: The most effective first-line pharmacological treatment for acute and subacute non-specific back pain and muscle strain — providing both analgesia and anti-inflammatory action. More effective than paracetamol for acute LBP.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.dosage: 400-600 mg three times daily with food; maximum 2400 mg/day; standard course 5-10 days for acute back pain
medicines.use_case: First-line NSAID for acute and subacute back pain; also excellent for inflammatory arthritis flares; widely available and well-tolerated at standard doses in young healthy adults
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor — reduces prostaglandin synthesis (anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic); reduces oedema and pain sensitisation around injured tissue
medicines.gastroprotection: Prescribe omeprazole or lansoprazole 20 mg once daily when ibuprofen used for >5 days, in elderly, or in those with prior GI history
contraindications: Peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
side_effects: Peptic ulcer and GI bleeding (especially in elderly, concurrent steroid use)
Cardiovascular risk with prolonged high-dose use

medicines.name: Diclofenac
medicines.dosage: 50 mg three times daily with food; or 75 mg slow-release twice daily; maximum 150 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Highly effective for acute musculoskeletal pain and back pain; more potent analgesic than ibuprofen at therapeutic doses; diclofenac injection 75 mg IM for acute severe back pain when oral route not possible
medicines.mechanism: Preferential COX-2 inhibitor (some COX-1 activity); particularly effective for musculoskeletal and soft tissue pain
medicines.side_effects: Similar to ibuprofen; slightly higher cardiovascular risk than ibuprofen or naproxen at high doses
medicines.note: Diclofenac SR 75 mg twice daily is a commonly prescribed and effective formulation for subacute and chronic back pain

medicines.name: Naproxen
medicines.dosage: 250-500 mg twice daily with food; maximum 1000 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Effective NSAID for back pain with the advantage of twice-daily dosing (better adherence); lower cardiovascular risk profile than diclofenac or COX-2 inhibitors; useful in patients with mild cardiovascular risk
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective COX inhibitor with slightly longer half-life than ibuprofen
medicines.side_effects: Similar to ibuprofen; long half-life means GI effects may persist if discontinued

medicines.name: Etoricoxib (COX-2 Selective Inhibitor)
medicines.dosage: 60-90 mg once daily (60 mg for chronic LBP; 90 mg for acute)
medicines.use_case: First-line NSAID for patients with GI risk (prior peptic ulcer, GI bleed, elderly) — selective COX-2 inhibition spares gastric mucosa; once-daily dosing; highly effective for acute and chronic back pain, disc pain, and spondylosis; widely used in India
medicines.mechanism: Highly selective COX-2 inhibitor — preferentially inhibits inflammatory prostaglandins; minimal gastric mucosal effect (spares COX-1 protective prostaglandins)
contraindications: Cardiovascular disease (ischaemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) — increased MI and stroke risk with COX-2 inhibitors
side_effects: GI side effects significantly less than non-selective NSAIDs
Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke) with long-term use in high-risk patients

medicines.name: Celecoxib
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: GI-sparing NSAID for patients at GI risk; effective for chronic spondylosis, ankylosing spondylitis, and inflammatory back pain; slightly lower cardiovascular risk than etoricoxib among COX-2 inhibitors
medicines.note: Cross-reactivity with sulphonamide allergy — check allergy history

categories.category_name: Topical Analgesics — Local Treatment for Localised Back Pain
categories.purpose: Topical preparations deliver analgesic and anti-inflammatory agents directly to the affected site, providing effective pain relief with minimal systemic absorption and fewer side effects than oral medications. Particularly useful for mild-moderate localised back pain.

medicines.name: Topical Diclofenac (Gel, Spray, or Patch)
medicines.dosage: Apply 2-4 g (cherry-sized amount) to the painful area 3-4 times daily; rub in gently; avoid broken skin; wash hands after application
medicines.use_case: First-line for localised back pain (strain, muscle spasm, facet joint pain) — excellent evidence for efficacy; comparable to oral NSAIDs for localised pain with significantly fewer GI side effects; particularly suitable for elderly patients, those with renal disease, and those who cannot tolerate oral NSAIDs
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs and systematic reviews confirm topical diclofenac is effective for acute and chronic musculoskeletal pain (Cochrane 2012); systemic absorption approximately 6% of equivalent oral dose

medicines.name: Topical Ibuprofen Gel
medicines.dosage: Apply 4-10 cm ribbon to affected area up to 4 times daily
medicines.use_case: Localised muscle strain and back pain; OTC availability; good evidence for efficacy in acute soft tissue injuries

medicines.name: Capsaicin Cream / Patch (0.025% - 8%)
medicines.dosage: Low-concentration cream: apply thin layer 3-4 times daily to painful area; burning sensation initially (substance P depletion — expected and diminishes with continued use); apply for minimum 4 weeks before assessing benefit
medicines.use_case: Chronic back pain and chronic musculoskeletal pain — depletes substance P from peripheral nociceptors; particularly useful for chronic myofascial pain and neuropathic components; evidence for both low-concentration cream (mild) and high-concentration patch (8% — specialist-applied for refractory chronic pain; effects last 3-6 months)
medicines.mechanism: Capsaicin activates and then desensitises TRPV1 receptors on peripheral nociceptors — initial burning followed by prolonged analgesic desensitisation; depletes substance P (pain neurotransmitter) from C-fibres
side_effects: Intense burning sensation at application site (expected — warn patient)
Avoid contact with eyes and mucous membranes

medicines.name: Lidocaine Patches (5% Topical)
medicines.dosage: Apply 1-3 patches to the most painful area for 12 hours on / 12 hours off daily
medicines.use_case: Localised chronic back pain and myofascial pain; particularly useful for allodynia (pain from non-painful touch) over a specific area; neuropathic back pain; chronic paraspinal muscle tenderness
medicines.mechanism: Topical local anaesthetic — stabilises peripheral nociceptor membranes; reduces ectopic discharge from sensitised nociceptors; minimal systemic absorption

medicines.name: Methyl Salicylate (Wintergreen) + Menthol Topical Preparations
medicines.dosage: Apply generously to affected area and massage gently 2-3 times daily; avoid broken skin
medicines.use_case: Widely used traditional topical analgesics for acute and subacute muscle strain and back pain; methyl salicylate provides mild anti-inflammatory and rubefacient (warming) effect; menthol provides cooling counter-irritant sensation (activates cold receptors — competing with pain signals — gate control theory); limited scientific evidence for clinical superiority over placebo but widely used and generally safe
medicines.note: Despite limited RCT evidence, these preparations are widely used across India and many patients find them helpful; safe for short-term use; avoid excessive application (methyl salicylate is absorbed transdermally — toxicity possible with large amounts on broken skin or in children)

categories.purpose: Simple analgesic for back pain — safer than NSAIDs for patients with GI, renal, or cardiovascular risk. Evidence for acute LBP is weaker than NSAIDs but it provides useful background analgesia when combined with NSAIDs or physical measures.

medicines.name: Paracetamol
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500-1000 mg every 4-6 hours; maximum 4000 mg (4g) per day; 3000 mg/day maximum in liver disease, frailty, or low body weight
medicines.use_case: Back pain where NSAIDs are contraindicated (peptic ulcer, renal disease, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy); useful as add-on to NSAID for moderate-severe pain (multimodal analgesia); elderly patients as first-line preference
medicines.mechanism: Central analgesic (inhibits prostaglandin synthesis centrally; possible serotonergic and endocannabinoid mechanisms); NOT anti-inflammatory at standard doses — no significant peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
side_effects: Hepatotoxicity with overdose — most common cause of acute liver failure in the UK; ALWAYS stay within 4g/day maximum
medicines.evidence_note: A 2014 Lancet study (PACE trial) found paracetamol no more effective than placebo for acute low back pain — however it remains widely recommended as an adjunct and for patients where NSAIDs are contraindicated

categories.category_name: Muscle Relaxants — Short-Term Symptomatic Treatment of Spasm
categories.purpose: Reduce painful muscle spasm in acute back pain — breaking the pain-spasm-pain cycle that perpetuates acute strain. Should be prescribed for SHORT COURSES ONLY (maximum 5-7 days). Not indicated for chronic back pain.
categories.warning: All muscle relaxants cause sedation — do NOT drive or operate machinery; alcohol significantly potentiates sedative effects; dependency and misuse risk with benzodiazepines (diazepam); do NOT prescribe routinely or for more than 7 days

medicines.name: Diazepam (Benzodiazepine Muscle Relaxant)
medicines.dosage: 2-5 mg at night (or 2 mg twice daily in severe spasm); MAXIMUM 5 days — strict limit
medicines.use_case: Severe acute muscle spasm with significant pain — most effective for short-term muscle relaxation; also anxiolytic (helpful when anxiety component worsening spasm); combined with physiotherapy for acute spasm
medicines.mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor activity — central nervous system depressant; reduces muscle stretch reflex sensitivity through spinal interneuron inhibition
side_effects: Physical dependence and withdrawal (even after short courses)
medicines.critical_note: Maximum 5-day course ONLY — benzodiazepine dependence can begin within 2-4 weeks of regular use; never prescribe for chronic back pain; will not solve pain — only temporary spasm relief to allow early movement

medicines.name: Methocarbamol
medicines.dosage: 1500 mg four times daily for first 2-3 days; then 750 mg four times daily; maximum 5-7 day course
medicines.use_case: Acute muscle spasm and back pain; centrally acting muscle relaxant without the dependency risk of benzodiazepines; preferred over diazepam for muscle spasm in patients with substance use history
medicines.mechanism: Central nervous system depressant — mechanism not fully established; reduces polysynaptic reflexes in spinal cord

medicines.name: Tizanidine (Centrally Acting Alpha-2 Agonist)
medicines.dosage: 2-4 mg at night initially; titrate up to 8-16 mg per day in 2-4 divided doses; maximum 36 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Muscle spasm in both acute back pain and spastic conditions (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy); particularly useful for patients where benzodiazepines are contraindicated; also mildly analgesic
medicines.mechanism: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist at spinal level — inhibits release of excitatory amino acids from spinal interneurons; reduces muscle tone centrally
side_effects: Hypotension (especially first dose — advise sitting to standing slowly)
Liver enzyme elevation (monitor LFTs in prolonged use)

medicines.name: Baclofen (GABA-B Agonist)
medicines.dosage: 5 mg three times daily initially; increase gradually to 10-20 mg three times daily; maximum 80 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Muscle spasm particularly from neurological causes (spinal cord injury, MS, cerebral palsy); also used for musculoskeletal back pain spasm; generally requires titration over weeks
medicines.mechanism: GABA-B receptor agonist at presynaptic level — inhibits motor neuron firing in spinal cord; reduces muscle stretch reflexes
side_effects: Muscle weakness (can unmask weakness if over-prescribed)
ABRUPT WITHDRAWAL RISK: never stop suddenly — seizures, hallucinations; always taper slowly

categories.category_name: Neuropathic Analgesics — For Radicular Pain (Sciatica) Specifically
categories.purpose: Evidence-based treatment for nerve root pain (sciatica, radiculopathy) — reduce the burning, shooting, electric-shock type pain of nerve root irritation and compression. NOT effective for non-specific mechanical back pain.

medicines.name: Gabapentin
medicines.dosage: Start 300 mg at night (night 1); 300 mg twice daily (day 2); 300 mg three times daily (day 3); titrate slowly over 2-4 weeks to effective dose (usually 900-3600 mg/day in 3 divided doses); reduce dose in renal impairment
medicines.use_case: Radicular pain (sciatica) from lumbar disc herniation or spinal stenosis; cervical radiculopathy; post-herpetic neuralgia; diabetic neuropathic pain; central sensitisation in chronic back pain
medicines.mechanism: Binds to alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in central and peripheral nervous system — reduces neuronal excitability and ectopic firing of sensitised or compressed nerve roots; reduces central sensitisation
side_effects: Sedation and dizziness (most common — dose-related; take at night initially)
Abuse potential (monitor — risk of misuse for sedation/euphoria at high doses)
medicines.note: Start LOW — go SLOW titration essential to minimise side effects; effect on radicular pain takes 2-4 weeks to assess; if no benefit at 1800-2400 mg/day, unlikely to benefit

medicines.name: Pregabalin
medicines.dosage: 75 mg twice daily initially; increase to 150 mg twice daily after 3-7 days; maximum 300 mg twice daily (600 mg/day); reduce dose in renal impairment
medicines.use_case: Radicular pain (sciatica, cervical radiculopathy); fibromyalgia; generalised anxiety disorder (co-prescribed for anxiety component of chronic pain); neuropathic pain; similar to gabapentin but more predictable absorption
medicines.mechanism: Same mechanism as gabapentin (alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit binding) but better oral bioavailability and more predictable pharmacokinetics
side_effects: Higher abuse and dependence potential than gabapentin — controlled substance in UK; monitor prescribing
medicines.note: NHS England has flagged pregabalin misuse — caution in patients with substance use history; regularly review ongoing need

categories.purpose: Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) and SNRIs (duloxetine) have evidence for reducing chronic back pain independently of their antidepressant effect — through descending pain pathway modulation. Also treat the commonly co-existing depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance in chronic back pain.

medicines.name: Amitriptyline (Tricyclic Antidepressant at Low Dose)
medicines.dosage: 10-25 mg at night (analgesic dose — much lower than antidepressant dose of 75-150 mg); may increase to 75 mg at night if tolerated and needed; take 1-2 hours before bedtime
medicines.use_case: Chronic non-specific back pain; chronic radicular pain; fibromyalgia; concurrent insomnia and depression with chronic back pain; central sensitisation; neuropathic components of chronic pain
medicines.mechanism: Noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition — strengthens descending pain inhibitory pathways from periaqueductal grey matter to spinal dorsal horn; at low analgesic doses: sedation (antihistamine H1 effect) improves sleep; also anticholinergic
side_effects: Sedation — beneficial for sleep (take at night)
Cardiac conduction effects (QTc prolongation — ECG if cardiac history)
medicines.note: Analgesic effect begins within 1-2 weeks (faster than antidepressant effect which takes 4-6 weeks); inform patients the dose prescribed is much lower than doses used for depression — prevents stigma concern

medicines.name: Duloxetine (SNRI — Serotonin-Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor)
medicines.dosage: 30 mg once daily for 1 week; increase to 60 mg once daily (standard dose); maximum 120 mg/day (divided doses)
medicines.use_case: Chronic low back pain (one of few medications with consistent RCT evidence specifically for chronic LBP — NICE 2016 recommends duloxetine); co-existing depression and anxiety with chronic back pain; fibromyalgia; diabetic peripheral neuropathy (common comorbidity); radicular pain
medicines.mechanism: Equal inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake — enhances descending pain inhibitory pathways; noradrenergic component particularly important for musculoskeletal pain modulation
side_effects: Nausea (most common — take with food; usually settles within 2 weeks)
Discontinuation syndrome if stopped abruptly — always taper
medicines.evidence: NICE (2016) and ACP (American College of Physicians 2017) guidelines both recommend duloxetine for chronic LBP as one of the few medications with consistent evidence

categories.purpose: Provide analgesia for severe acute back pain uncontrolled by NSAIDs and paracetamol. Opioids have a very limited and controversial role in chronic back pain — risks of dependence, tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and disability outweigh modest long-term benefits.
